Tirante beat Tabilo 7–5, 7–6 in the SF to reach his first tour-level final, though Tabilo still leads their head to head after 3 meetings. It was a tight match decided by a few points at the end of each set.

Tirante was dominant on serve early and dropped just one point in his first service games. A single break decided the first set: he broke for 6–5, had to save 3 break points when he served for the set and still held for 7–5. That was the moment of the match. In the second set he broke for 5–4 but nerves got in the way when he served for the match and Tabilo broke straight back. Tirante stayed with it and took the tiebreak 7–1. On that game at 5–4, he said: "Well, always we have nervous all the matches … I think I keep believing in me, in my team"

The serve won him this match. Tirante won 90% of his first-serve points (!!!) and Tabilo found almost no answer to it. Behind that he moved forward at the earliest chance and finished points at the net, while most of his winners came from the forehand.

Tabilo showed good touch and used the whole court but at times his shot choices were unclear and some of his volleys were not good enough. His forehand was the weak side, with 15 unforced errors there.

Physically, Tirante is something to follow. He called the physio early in the second set, his second medical timeout in two matches. We do not know the reason yet.

All in all, a strong win from Tirante, the attacking baseliner, built on his serve and on a game that took him forward whenever he could. He has now played 4 tiebreaks this week, so close finishes are nothing new for him. His second medical timeout this week is something to follow before the final. Shevchenko kept fighting with belief and the second set followed the same path, with no break and a tiebreak he won 7–5 this time.

Shevchenko had a tight turnaround after a match that ended around quarter past ten the night before. He converted none of his 3 break points in the third set. That made the difference in the end.

Rune beat Kecmanovic 2–6, 6–1, 6–4 in R2 and now leads their head to head 4 wins to 1. It was a comeback from a set down in the last match of the day in Stockholm, late at night.

Rune made many errors from the start, while Kecmanovic hit hard off the forehand, broke for 1–0 and again for 4–1 and did not have to do much to take the set with a double break. Even when Rune followed one slow first serve to the net, a Kecmanovic forehand passed him. On the first set, Rune said: "I think I was just a bit overwhelmed."

That changed early in the second set. Rune broke for 3–1, broke again for 5–1 and won 7 games in a row from 1–1. From there the match turned completely. In the third set he needed 2 break points to break for 1–0 and Kecmanovic broke back for 2–2 but Rune broke again for 5–4 and won the next game to finish it.

After the first set Rune hardly missed a ball, returned very well and used his serve to set up points. The return made the difference: he won 61% of the points against the second serve, far above his usual 50%. His forehand was all or nothing, with most of his winners and most of his errors on that side.

Kecmanovic stayed solid on his own serve for a long time but once Rune settled he saved only 1 of 5 break points.

All in all, a strong comeback from Rune, built on his return and his attacking baseline game, which suits the medium pace of this indoor court in Stockholm. Next is Fritz, the number one seed, who has not dropped a set this week and beat Norrie in straight sets.

Shevchenko beat Ruud 6–7 (tiebreak 7–5), 6–4, 6–3 in R2 and the head to head now reads Shevchenko 1, Ruud 2. The qualifier came from a set down in a long match that turned on a few big points.

The first set could easily have gone the other way. Shevchenko needed 2 break points to break for 6–5, then Ruud saved 1 set point and broke straight back for 6–6 when Shevchenko served for the set. Ruud took the tiebreak 7–5 with a shot that came more off the frame than the strings.

The moment of the match came early in the second set, when Shevchenko saved 2 break points and held for 3–2. He moved on quickly from the lost first set and at 5–4 he broke Ruud to take the set 6–4. In the third set he broke for 3–1 and got broken back for 2–3 but broke again for 5–3. He finished the match with a backhand.

Shevchenko won it with his serve and his game from the back of the court. He won 79% of his first-serve points, well above his career average on hard. In the rallies he was clearly the better player, with strong forehands and plenty of time on the ball. He sums it up himself: "I played at a good level. I kept being aggressive the whole match. I'm really happy now"

Ruud struggled to land his first serve, at only 60%, well below his usual level. His forehand was high risk and high reward: most of his winners and most of his unforced errors came from that wing.

There is one physical point to follow for Ruud. He called the physio twice: late in the first set and early in the second set. We do not know the reason yet. Something to follow for the next tournaments of Ruud.

All in all, a strong comeback from Shevchenko, built on his serve and an attacking baseline game that suits a medium-paced indoor court like Stockholm. Fritz beat Norrie 7–5, 6–3 in R2 to reach the quarterfinals in Stockholm and he now leads their head to head 9 wins to 6. It was a first set that Norrie came very close to winning, then a calm second set from the number one seed.

Norrie started better. He dictated with his forehand, returned well and broke for 2–1. He saved 2 break points to hold for 5–3 and served for the set at 5–4, where Fritz saved 2 set points and broke back for 5–5 on his second break point of the game. From there the match turned completely: Fritz saved 2 break points to hold for 6–5 and broke again for 7–5, winning 5 games in a row from 3–5 down. Fritz described it like this: "I feel like there were a lot of times in the first set when I lost some big points, I had some chances, … Towards the end of that set, I started winning some of those big points. I played really well, got the momentum and finished the set." In the second set Norrie saved 1 break point to hold for 1–1. Fritz then broke for 5–3 and closed out the match with his 13th ace.

Fritz won it on return as much as on serve. He won 42% of the points against the first serve, far above his 27% average on hard. As his forehand warmed up, he stepped in to take the ball early and was clearly the better player from the baseline.

Norrie played well early on but could do very little against the Fritz serve, especially out wide. He won only 19% of the points against the first serve.

All in all, a strong comeback from Fritz, built on his return and on a forehand that got better and better. As a big server and complete baseliner, he can hurt opponents from everywhere. Next is Rune, who beat Bergs in straight sets and then Kecmanovic in three sets after losing the first set.

Tabilo beat Sonego 7–6, 6–7, 7–5 in R2 in Stockholm to reach the QF and now has 2 wins to Sonego's 1 in their 3 meetings. It was a long match of almost three hours in which the serve ruled and only one break of serve came at all.

The danger came right at the start. Tabilo had to save 3 break points in the opening game before he held for 1–0 and nobody broke after that, so he took the first set 7–2 in the tiebreak. The second set went the same way: Sonego saved 1 break point to hold for 6–5 and then won a long tiebreak 9–7. The third set looked like another tiebreak until Tabilo broke for 7–5 in the very last game. That was the moment of the match. Tabilo said: "It was just a very tough match. I think we were both serving very well. There was no break until there at the end, so it was just tough mentally."

Once again he won it with his serve. Tabilo won 81% of his first-serve points, well above his 73% average on hard and Sonego never broke him after that first game. From the baseline he was clearly the better player, with his forehand doing most of the damage. It was not his best return performance, so the one break at the end was all he needed.

Sonego had come through qualifying and played well for long spells. He used his forehand to push Tabilo off balance and then came forward to finish points at the net. But he took none of his 3 break points in the opening game and got no other chance to break.

All in all, a tight win from Tabilo built on his serve, which makes this attacking baseliner dangerous on a medium-paced indoor court like this one. Next is Michelsen, who has not dropped a set this week and beat Hanfmann and Cerundolo in straight sets on the way.

Samuel beat Borg 6–3, 6–2 in R1 in their first meeting. It started badly for him but became more and more one-sided as it went on.

Borg broke in the very first game for 1–0. Samuel needed 2 break points but broke straight back for 1–1, then broke again for 5–3 and closed the first set 6–3. The second set was harder work on return than the score suggests. Samuel needed 4 break points to break for 3–2. That was the moment of the match, because it was part of a run of 5 games in a row that ended the match. He needed 4 more break points to break again for 5–2. Borg saved 1 match point in the next game with Samuel serving at 5–2 but he served it out.

He won it with his serve. Samuel won 78% of the points behind his first serve and after the break in the first game Borg never got another chance to break. When Samuel came forward it worked too: he did not lose a single point at the net.

Borg gave too much away on his own serve. He made 6 double faults and that kept handing Samuel chances on return.

All in all, a solid win from Samuel after a poor start. It was built on his serve and on finishing points when he had the chance, which fits his attacking baseline game. The one thing to improve is the return in the big moments, where he needed a lot of chances to break. Next is Musetti in R2.

Etcheverry beat Dahlin 6–4, 6–7, 6–3 in R1, in their first meeting. It was a long fight against an opponent who held his serve under pressure again and again and took the match to a third set.

Etcheverry broke right away for 1–0, although he needed 3 break points in that game and that one break carried him through the first set. Dahlin saved a set point at 5–3 on his own serve but Etcheverry still took the set 6–4. The second set had no break of serve at all: Dahlin saved a break point when he held for 4–3 and another one when he held for 5–4, then won the tiebreak to level the match.

In the third set Dahlin saved one more break point to hold for 2–2 but Etcheverry finally broke for 5–3. Dahlin even saved a match point with Etcheverry serving at 5–3 before Etcheverry closed it 6–3. Etcheverry gave his opponent credit: "It was a tough match for me. He is an incredible young player and he has an incredible future ahead of him"

He won it with his serve. Etcheverry landed 85% of his first serves, far above his 65% average on hard and he did not face a single break point in the whole match. It was not his best return performance, with only 2 of 8 break points converted.

Dahlin kept it close for two sets but his first serve let him down when it mattered most, with only 40% landed in the third set. Dahlin still took a lot from the day: "Very cool experience of course, it was a fantastic atmosphere. I started the match a bit slowly but got going afterwards."

All in all, a hard-earned win for Etcheverry. His serve held from start to finish and his solid baseline game gave him the one break he needed in the third set. The medium-paced indoor court in Stockholm suited his serve well.
